title: Purpose of a second interview; preserving the family's life story
description: The interviewer asks what a second interview would be like and whether Isabel had ever told her whole life story before. Isabel says she had not, and explains that her husband wanted the recording kept for their children and was disappointed when early plans for it fell through.

title: Transcription costs; using interviews for research
description: They discuss how time-consuming transcription is, citing Sam Schrager's estimate of ten hours of work per hour of tape, and note that researchers need paper transcripts even though tapes preserve the speaker's flavor. The interviewer explains how answers grouped by topic, such as child rearing and the importance of work, can be analyzed to characterize the lives of women in northern Idaho.

title: Forty years in the valley; changes in neighborhood life
description: Isabel recalls organizing celebrations for her fortieth wedding anniversary and her early need to meet other people when houses were scarce and neighbors depended on one another. They agree that cars and new housing have made communities less close-knit, and she describes her efforts to organize neighbors and hold gatherings.

title: Effects of being interviewed; women's unrecognized contributions
description: Isabel says the first interview brought back many memories and she wishes she had written things down, while the interviewer wishes her own grandfather had recorded his story. They reflect on how women dismiss their everyday work as unexceptional and how important it is for later generations to recognize how much mothers did and how hard their lives were.

title: Continuing education; women's learning clubs
description: Asked what would have improved her life, Isabel says further education, and describes herself as a charter member who instigated a learning club using university materials and programs on nutrition. They discuss how rural women have fewer opportunities than women in a college town like Moscow, and how social groups once mattered more when there was no television or radio.

title: Living without power; schoolhouse as social center
description: They speculate about how people would cope if gasoline and power were cut off, agreeing that younger people would adapt. Isabel remembers literary programs at the country school, entertaining teachers, church activities, and notes that she attended, and later taught at, the same school her husband had attended.

title: Value of rural women's stories; Elk River fire tales
description: The speakers talk about the pleasure of hearing stories from rural women in the Midwest and the value of recording them. They recount Roy McKinney's stories of a fire near Elk River and Kellogg, including men who escaped the flames by getting down into the water.

title: The old schoolhouse; teaching and family dates
description: Isabel talks about the schoolhouse, recalling that she went through grade school and high school there and returned to teach for four years in the early 1930s. She mentions her family arriving in the area around 1907, her post office work, and finishing school in 1918, and notes her husband attended the same school earlier.

title: Portrait photographs; capturing older women's character
description: The interviewer asks Isabel how she felt about being photographed, and both note that nearly everyone protests at first. They agree that photographs of older people convey a spirit the voice alone cannot, with faces and hands made beautiful by a life of work, and that seeing the picture together with hearing the voice brings the person to life.

title: Crocheting, quilting, and women's handwork
description: They talk about Isabel's crocheting and quilt making, joking about thousands of potholders and dozens of sweaters made over the years. The interviewer admires how active older women remain, while Isabel suggests younger people today are simply too busy for such handwork.

title: Changing work of women; influence on public life
description: Isabel compares the domestic work of women in the past with younger women's greater freedom through cars and activities outside the home, including daughters who help drive trucks at harvest while still canning and gardening. Asked about women's say in government, she says women in the past left decisions to men but exerted real influence through their husbands and families.

title: Advice for newcomers; small-town life today
description: The interviewer asks what advice Isabel would give a city person moving to a town like Elk River, and Isabel says newcomers should make themselves known and let people approach them. She describes the town as friendly, with a good grocery store and school, and not a bad place to live.

title: Small-town community; role of churches
description: The speaker discusses how churches historically functioned as the central institution for social integration in small towns. They explain that this was the primary way people became part of their community and got acquainted, though they are uncertain whether this remains true today. The speaker mentions their own lifelong church involvement and that of their family.
